title: Psychology and Development: Applications from Cognitive and Social Psychology
venue: Handbook of Development Economics (NBER Working Paper 34753)
tldr: A missing markets framework explains why psychological constraints---self-control, limited cognition, self-beliefs, mental health, and social norms---amplify poverty and shape markets and institutions in developing countries.
problem_and_motivation: Development economics has focused on external constraints such as missing markets and weak institutions, while internal psychological constraints---the behavioral biases common to all people---have received less attention in the context of poverty. The field lacks a systematic understanding of whether these psychological channels meaningfully impede individuals' ability to climb out of poverty and shape the functioning of markets in developing countries. Existing reviews have not fully explored why behavioral biases matter more in low-income settings or how poverty-specific features amplify their consequences.
approach: Proposes a missing markets framework explaining why markets fail to supply behavioral aids---tools, products, or services that mitigate psychological constraints---due to consumer naivete, firm incentives to exploit biases, unobserved heterogeneity, and contracting frictions.

Identifies five features of poverty---proximity to subsistence, high volatility, market failures, weak institutions, and reliance on social ties---that amplify the consequences of psychological constraints.

Reviews empirical evidence across five psychological constructs: self-control, cognitive constraints, self-beliefs, mental health, and social norms, organized around how each interacts with the conditions of poverty.
Surveys field experiments offering hard and soft commitment devices, including lockboxes, ROSCAs, and naturally occurring illiquidity arrangements, to test for demand for commitment.
Examines how environmental stressors such as heat, noise, and sleep deprivation, as well as physiological stressors from early childhood, affect cognitive function among the poor.
Reviews evidence on cognitive constraints including selective attention, the planning fallacy, recency bias, and mental accounting in developing country settings.
Analyzes psychosocial interventions targeting self-beliefs, aspirations, self-efficacy, and growth mindset through workshops, role model videos, and CBT-based programs.
Surveys mental health interventions including CBT and behavioral activation therapy for depression and anxiety, and trauma-focused interventions for PTSD-affected populations.
Examines social norms enforcement mechanisms including price collusion, the social tax from redistributive pressures, inter-group stereotypes, and the contact hypothesis.
Argues for complementary research approaches combining clean experimental tests of mechanisms with messier studies rooted in observed real-world behavior.

num: Worker output rises 8% from the beginning to the end of the pay week, consistent with present-biased self-control problems in labor effort.
num: Farmers in Kenya were far from the yield-maximizing pod size despite years of experience, documenting how selective attention leads to large productivity losses.
num: Prompts to think through future expenses associatively increased recall of future expenses by 43%, leading to 20% higher savings and 9% higher yields at year-end.
num: 93% of refugee households opted in to receive cash in labeled envelopes, leading to higher investments and income one year later.
num: Receiving an early cash transfer before a high-stakes exam increased college attendance by 0.7 percentage points and formal-sector employment by 1 percentage point.
num: Cash infusion increased worker productivity by 7% mediated by decreased attentional mistakes, consistent with improved cognition from reduced financial strain.
num: Workers with above-mean payday effects were 49% more likely to select dominated commitment contracts and experienced a 9% increase in output.
num: Psychotherapy intervention for prenatal depression in Pakistan led to 0.2-0.3 standard deviation increases in financial and time investments in children.

num: Aspiration workshop participants in Kenya had higher labor supply, investment, revenue, and living standards 17 months later, but the workshop had no incremental benefit conditional on receiving a cash transfer.
num: Agricultural workers take-up of below-prevailing-wage jobs plummets from 33% to 1.8% under social observability, but rises to 26% when offers are private.
num: Treated students who practiced focusing for 10-20 hours over an academic year improved grades by 0.09 standard deviations in Hindi, English, and Math.

topics.name: Financial Behavior of Filipino Young Professionals
topics.justification: Self-control and cognitive constraints in savings, borrowing, and spending behavior among low-income individuals provide behavioral foundations relevant to financial decision-making.

topics.name: Culturally Specific Financial Practices
topics.justification: ROSCAs and informal savings institutions are reviewed as prominent culturally embedded financial institutions reflecting demand for commitment.

topics.name: Financial Behavioral Profiles in Personal Finance Systems
topics.justification: Heterogeneity in self-control problems, cognitive constraints, and self-beliefs documented across individuals provides evidence for distinct behavioral profiles.

topics.name: Budgeting Strategies as Domain Knowledge
topics.justification: Mental accounting and planning fallacy findings inform how individuals allocate spending across categories, though not framed as budgeting systems.

topics.name: Budget Recommendation in Personal Finance Systems
topics.justification: Behavioral aids such as commitment devices and mental accounting tools serve analogous roles to budget recommendations, but are not presented as automated systems.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This handbook chapter provides a comprehensive research agenda for behavioral development economics, synthesizing evidence on how psychological constraints interact with poverty to shape individual behavior and institutional outcomes. It introduces the missing markets framework as a rationale for why markets fail to supply behavioral aids and why policy intervention is justified to correct these missing markets rather than as paternalism. The review organizes evidence across five core psychological constructs---self-control, cognitive constraints, self-beliefs, mental health, and social norms---and highlights where proof of concept exists versus meaningful economic impacts. It identifies five features of development that amplify the consequences of behavioral biases and proposes complementary research directions combining controlled experiments with observation of real-world behavior.
directly_justifies: Psychological constraints such as self-control problems and limited attention are especially consequential in developing country settings with high volatility and missing markets.
Mental accounting---the tendency to categorize money into separate accounts---is routinely used by low-income individuals and can be leveraged through labeled savings tools.
Soft commitment devices relying on social pressure or psychological costs can be comparable or more effective than hard commitment devices in one-shot interventions.
Heterogeneity in self-control problems across individuals creates stable differences in demand for commitment and productivity outcomes.
Financial concerns capture bottom-up attention, potentially reducing cognitive bandwidth available for other tasks, though evidence remains mixed.
limits: The review is organized by psychological construct rather than by application domain, limiting direct mapping to specific financial system design requirements.
Most evidence comes from experimental interventions rather than observational studies of existing behavior, limiting external validity for system-level design.
The cross-country reversal of the mental health-income relationship within-country remains unexplained, introducing uncertainty about mental health mechanisms.
The review explicitly notes that much of the literature remains at proof of concept rather than demonstrating first-order impacts on poverty.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned for relevance. Domains 1.C, 2.A, 5.A, 7.A, and 7.B were flagged as having at least tangential relevance: 1.C and 2.A for financial behavior and culturally embedded practices like ROSCAs; 5.A for heterogeneity in self-control and cognitive profiles; 7.A and 7.B for mental accounting and commitment devices as budgeting aids. Domains 1.A, 1.B, 2.B-2.D, 3.A-3.C, 4.A-4.B, 5.B-5.C, 6.A-6.B, 7.C-7.E, 8.A-8.C, 9.A-9.C, 10.A-10.C, 11.A-11.B, 12.A-12.C, 13.A-13.C, 14.A-14.C were considered and rejected because the paper does not address Filipino demographics, expense categorization, existing personal finance systems, predictive modeling, budgeting optimization, anomaly detection, mobile-first design, data privacy, engagement mechanics, evaluation frameworks, savings goal management, debt management, synthetic data generation, or model deployment. The paper is primarily a theoretical review chapter for the Handbook of Development Economics rather than an empirical study focused on personal finance system design, so most taxonomy domains are outside its scope.

limitations: The review is organized by psychological construct rather than by application domain, limiting direct applicability to system design.
Much of the evidence base consists of proof-of-concept field experiments rather than first-order evidence on poverty perpetuation.
Replication challenges exist for priming interventions and cognitive test measures across developing country settings.
The cross-country reversal of mental health-income correlations remains unresolved, creating uncertainty about mental health mechanisms.
remember_this: Behavioral biases matter more in poverty due to five features: proximity to subsistence, high volatility, market failures, weak institutions, and reliance on social ties.
